title: A Catholic doubter
hook: he remained Catholic and died during Mass in 1592, while doubting nearly everything else

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the wars: Montaigne kept his gate open and said the same plain words to both sides. Your line was talk to both.

A pair of scales, two pans hanging level. Montaigne took that image as his emblem, he says, with a short question beside it: what do I know? The same man submitted his writing to the judgment of the Church he was born in. He put the doubt and the faith in the same book, and hid neither one. Readers still argue about him, and about what that question left room for.
screen: `A PAIR OF BALANCED SCALES.` → `WHAT DO I KNOW?` → `AND STILL IN HIS CHURCH.`

segments.voice: First, the doubt. In the Apology for Raymond Sebond, Montaigne takes apart human confidence piece by piece. Our senses fool us. Our reason argues both sides of anything. Animals may know things we don't. Even the skeptics' own claim, I doubt, says too much, he thinks, because it sounds sure of itself. So he turns it into a question: what do I know? Second, the faith. In the essay Of prayers, he says he puts his thoughts forward as things to be explored, not truths to be believed, and submits them to the Church he was born in. He'd gladly see Christians use the Lord's Prayer at every turn. Third, how he holds them together, and here readers differ. Some read a sincere Catholic who thinks reason is too weak to reach God, so faith must come as a gift, not a proof. Some read the faith as a careful cover for a deeper doubt. Some say we simply can't see inside him, which would suit him well. Fourth, the end. Tradition says Montaigne died while Mass was being said in his room: the doubter, at the end, inside the rite of his church. Whatever you make of him, he didn't think faith and doubt had to evict each other. A scale doesn't need one pan empty to hang level.
screen: `OUR SENSES AND REASON FOOL US.` · `SUBMITTED TO THE CHURCH.` · `SINCERE, OR A COVER?` · `MASS SAID IN HIS ROOM.` · then, large: `FAITH AND DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open, one on each knee, like the two pans of a scale. In one, place something you trust, whatever that is for you: a person, a practice, a belief, the sun coming up; in the other, a question you can't answer. Don't let either hand win; just feel the weight of both.
A Catholic doubter. Montaigne, who asked what do I know?, stayed in the Church he was born in, and tradition says he died during Mass. Today's word.
Your line: faith and doubt. He let them share a room, and neither one had to leave. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne differ on how to hold his doubt and his Catholic faith together: some read him as a sincere believer who thought reason could not reach God, others read the faith as a cover, and some leave the question open.

chat.says: Was Montaigne a believer or a doubter?
options: Both, in one book: he asked what do I know?, and submitted it to his Church.
A doubter; he left the Church after writing the Apology for Raymond Sebond.
A believer; he wrote that he never had a single doubt in his whole life.
chat.meaning: Montaigne asked what do I know? yet submitted his writing to the Church he was born in. Readers differ on how he held faith and doubt together.

Raymond Sebond.meaning: the writer whose book Montaigne's Apology sets out to defend

skeptics.meaning: thinkers who hold that sure knowledge may be out of reach

Mass.meaning: the Catholic Church's central act of worship

emblem.meaning: a picture chosen to stand for a person or idea

notes: The index hook gives a year (1592) for his death; under the claims rule the script gives no year, and frames the death during Mass as tradition, from an account by a friend after his death (Étienne Pasquier's letter). Confirm.
